screens.title: Interacting with On-Chain Programs from React
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how a connected React DApp calls a deployed Solana program. We'll follow a simple, practical path: install Anchor's client library, import the program IDL, create an AnchorProvider that uses the user's wallet to sign, and call instructions like create and increment on a counter program. This matter: calling programs is the moment your front end triggers immutable on-chain logic, so correctness and clear feedback matter. For example, when your user clicks to create a counter account, the app derives a program-owned address, builds the instruction, and asks the wallet to sign and submit it. A common misconception is that Anchor magically hides all account requirements; Anchor helps but you still must supply correct accounts, enough SOL for fees and rent, and the proper program ID. By the end of this chapter you will be able to wire a React component to an Anchor program, interpret common errors such as missing signers or IDL mismatches, and design retry and feedback flows for users. Think about how you will surface errors to a user who signs a transaction that later times out.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will construct and sign Solana transactions from a React client, use Anchor's client library to call program instructions, and manage confirmation, errors, and fees. Start with the practical: learning how Anchor converts your IDL into methods that build instructions, and how AnchorProvider wraps a Connection and your wallet's send function to sign and submit those transactions. For example, when you call program. methods. create(). accounts({...}). rpc(), Anchor uses the IDL to serialize arguments, but the connected wallet must still approve signing. A common misconception is assuming Anchor removes the need to supply accounts; Anchor needs the correct accounts listed in the IDL and correct program IDs. You'll also practice deriving PDAs for program-owned state and checking balances to cover rent and fees. Finally, you'll learn how to handle typical failure modes such as missing signer errors or IDL mismatches and surface clear messages to users. These skills let you move from reading on-chain data to actively updating program state in a secure, user-friendly way.

screens.title: Anchor client setup and IDL usage
screens.narratorSegment: This screen walks through the exact setup you need to call Anchor programs from React. Start by installing the client library with npm install @coral-xyz/anchor; this gives you anchor. Program and AnchorProvider utilities. The IDL is a JSON description of your program's instructions, accounts, and types. You typically copy the compiled file from target/idl into src/idl so your front-end can import it. To create a program client, you need three items: the IDL, the program's PublicKey, and an AnchorProvider. The AnchorProvider wraps your Connection and the wallet's sendTransaction so Anchor can request signing and submission. A concrete example: create a provider from the useConnection and useWallet hooks, then call new anchor. Program(idl, programId, provider). A common misconception is that passing a null provider is fine for read operations; while read-only RPC calls can use Connection directly, anchor. Program requires the provider to sign transactions invoked by methods. As a takeaway, treat the IDL as your contract's surface and AnchorProvider as the bridge that connects that surface to the user's wallet and the cluster. How will you organize your imports so the IDL and provider are available where you need them?

keyIdea.title: Anchor setup
keyIdea.text: Install @coral-xyz/anchor, import your program's IDL, and instantiate anchor.Program with an AnchorProvider that uses the user's wallet.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Anchor client setup
Why IDL and Provider matter

The IDL defines how Anchor serializes instruction data and which accounts each instruction requires. The AnchorProvider connects the IDL to a Connection and the user's wallet for signing and sending.

// Install
npm install @coral-xyz/anchor

// Import IDL and instantiate program
import * as anchor from '@coral-xyz/anchor';
import idl from '../idl/counter.json';
const programId = new anchor.web3.PublicKey('YOUR_PROGRAM_ID_HERE');

// Inside a component with connection and wallet
const provider = new anchor.AnchorProvider(connection, { publicKey, sendTransaction } as any, { commitment: 'confirmed' });
const program = new anchor.Program(idl as anchor.Idl, programId, provider);
Note: the type cast for the wallet in AnchorProvider is a common workaround in TypeScript; in production you may wrap the wallet to match Anchor's expected shape.
Example

Import your compiled counter.idl into src/idl, set programId to your deployed address, and create the anchor.Program once per app area that performs transactions.

Common mistake

Using an outdated IDL after program changes will produce incorrect instruction data and lead to signature or account validation errors on submission.

Key Takeaway

Anchor's IDL and AnchorProvider are the plumbing that turn method calls into signed transactions and submitted RPCs.

screens.title: From user action to confirmed transaction
screens.narratorSegment: Let's trace the complete lifecycle of a user-triggered action. First, the DApp responds to a user action — for example, clicking 'Create Counter Account.' The app derives any PDAs and gathers the required PublicKeys from the IDL. Second, the app uses anchor. Program or raw web3 constructs to build one or more instructions and adds them to a Transaction object. Third, the app requests the connected wallet to sign the transaction. The wallet may display a confirmation pop-up showing fees and required signatures. Fourth, the wallet returns a signed transaction and your app sends it to the Solana cluster via Connection. Finally, the app waits for confirmation with a commitment level such as 'confirmed' and reports success or error. A concrete example: creating a counter account derives counterPda from seed ["counter", userPubkey], then calls program. methods. create(). accounts({ counterAccount: counterPda, user: userPubkey }). rpc(); Anchor handles serialization, but the wallet must sign. A common misconception is that transaction submission is instantaneous; network congestion or missing funds can delay or fail the transaction. As a takeaway, design your UI to show approval, pending confirmation, and clear failure messages so the user understands each stage.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle
keyIdea.text: User action → derive accounts → build instruction → wallet signs → send to cluster → wait for confirmation.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Tx lifecycle
Step-by-step
  1. 1. User triggers action. Example: 'Create Counter Account'.
  2. 2. Derive PDAs and assemble accounts required by IDL.
  3. 3. Build instruction(s) and append to Transaction.
  4. 4. Request wallet signature; wallet shows fees and signers.
  5. 5. Send signed transaction and wait for confirmation.
Concrete snippet
// Anchor builds and sends
await program.methods
  .create()
  .accounts({
    counterAccount: counterPda,
    user: publicKey,
    systemProgram: anchor.web3.SystemProgram.programId,
  })
  .rpc();
Common pitfall

If the wallet lacks sufficient SOL for new account rent or compute fees, the transaction will fail. Always check balances before creating new accounts.

Key Takeaway

Design UI flows that clearly show approval, pending confirmation, and final success or error so users understand the blockchain delay and cost.

screens.title: Program Derived Addresses (PDAs)
screens.narratorSegment: Program Derived Addresses, or PDAs, are deterministic public keys generated from a program ID and a set of seeds. They are commonly used to create program-owned accounts without a private key. In our counter example, the PDA is derived from the seed bytes of the string 'counter' plus the user's public key. Concretely, the code calls PublicKey. findProgramAddressSync([Buffer. from('counter'), publicKey. toBuffer()], program. programId) and receives the PDA and bump. PDAs matter because they let the program control the account while letting the client deterministically find the address. A common misconception is to treat a PDA like a user-owned key; a PDA cannot sign like a regular keypair — instead the program acts on it. If you provide the wrong seeds or program ID when deriving the PDA, the client and program will refer to different addresses and transactions will fail. As a takeaway, always derive PDAs the same way in both client and program, document your seeds, and verify the PDA on-chain after creation so your front end can safely reference it. Program Derived Addresses (PDAs) means pdas are deterministic, program-owned addresses derived from seeds and the program id; they let programs own state without a private key.. In practical terms, deterministic, program-owned accounts used for state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: PDA concept
keyIdea.text: PDAs are deterministic, program-owned addresses derived from seeds and the program ID; they let programs own state without a private key.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › PDAs
What is a PDA?

A PDA is computed from seeds and a program ID and is owned by the program. It is not backed by a private key, so only the program can authorize actions on it.

// Derive PDA
const [counterPda] = PublicKey.findProgramAddressSync(
  [Buffer.from('counter'), publicKey.toBuffer()],
  program.programId
);
// counterPda is deterministic and program-owned
Concrete use

Use the PDA as the counterAccount referenced in your create and increment instructions so the program can store the count securely.

Misconception

PDAs are not keys. You cannot sign with a PDA; the program enforces operations on the PDA via instruction checks and program logic.

Key Takeaway

Derive PDAs identically in client and program. If derivation differs, account mismatches will cause transaction failures.

screens.title: Calling program.methods(...).rpc()
screens.narratorSegment: Anchor exposes an intuitive method chain for calling instructions: program. methods. (...). accounts(...). rpc(). This chain does several things: it serializes arguments according to the IDL, it sets the accounts required by the instruction, and it uses the AnchorProvider to sign and submit the transaction. For example, calling program. methods. create(). accounts({ counterAccount: counterPda, user: publicKey, systemProgram: anchor. web3. SystemProgram. programId, }). rpc() will build the instruction to create the counter account, request the user's signature, and await confirmation. A common mistake is omitting an account declared as isSigner: true in the IDL; this raises a missing signer error because the program expected that signature. Another gotcha is an IDL mismatch — if the on-chain program changed but your local IDL did not, the serialization will be wrong. When using rpc(), provide clear UI messaging: show an approval prompt, then a pending state, and finally success or a human-readable error. As a takeaway, rely on program. methods for convenience, but always double-check required accounts and keep your IDL in sync with deployed programs. Calling program.methods(...).rpc() means program.methods.<name>().accounts(...).rpc() serializes data from the idl, requests wallet signing via the provider, and submits the transaction.. In practical terms, how anchor turns idl methods into signed rpcs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: program.methods.<name>().accounts(...).rpc() serializes data from the IDL, requests wallet signing via the provider, and submits the transaction.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Calling rpc()
Example call
await program.methods
  .create()
  .accounts({
    counterAccount: counterPda,
    user: publicKey,
    systemProgram: anchor.web3.SystemProgram.programId,
  })

This single call builds the instruction from the IDL, requests wallet signing through AnchorProvider, and sends the signed transaction to the network.
Developer checklist
  • Keep IDL in sync with deployed program.
  • Provide all accounts declared in the IDL, especially signers.
  • Check wallet has funds before creating accounts that require rent.
  • Show clear UI states for approval, pending, and confirmation.
Key Takeaway

Use program.methods for convenience but validate accounts and IDL alignment to avoid runtime failures.

screens.title: Anchor vs manual web3.js calls
screens.narratorSegment: Anchor simplifies client-side interaction by generating type-safe method calls from your IDL, which reduces the need to manually serialize instruction data. Using anchor. Program gives you program. methods. (). accounts(...). rpc() that handles serialization, instruction creation, and uses the provided AnchorProvider to sign and send. In contrast, manual calls with @solana/web3. js require you to build TransactionInstruction objects, manually pack argument bytes, and manage which accounts are writable or signers. A concrete example: incrementing a counter using Anchor is a few chained calls and an rpc() call. Doing the same with web3. js means constructing the instruction data buffer exactly as the program expects. A common misconception is that Anchor removes the need to understand accounts and serialization; it does not. Anchor reduces boilerplate but you still must supply correct accounts and understand program constraints. Use Anchor for faster development and clearer client code; use manual web3. js when you need full control over bytes, custom serialization, or when interacting with programs that do not provide an IDL. The takeaway: prefer Anchor for Anchor-based programs, but keep familiarity with raw web3. js for edge cases and debugging.

keyIdea.title: Anchor vs web3.js
keyIdea.text: Anchor provides IDL-driven, type-safe calls; web3.js gives raw control. Use Anchor when available and web3.js for low-level needs.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Anchor vs web3.js
Anchor (IDL-based)
  • Type-safe methods generated from IDL
  • Handles serialization and instruction building
  • Integrates with AnchorProvider for signing
@solana/web3.js (manual)
  • Full control over instruction bytes
  • Requires manual packing of arguments
  • Useful for programs without an IDL or custom serialization
Example

Anchor: program.methods.increment().accounts({...}).rpc() — minimal client code. Manual: build TransactionInstruction with program id, keys, and serialized data buffer.

Key Takeaway

Prefer Anchor for Anchor programs for clarity and speed; use raw web3.js when you need low-level control or when no IDL exists.

screens.title: Handling transaction fees and rent
screens.narratorSegment: Transactions on Solana require small SOL payments to cover compute and the rent-exempt balance for new accounts. When your DApp creates a program-owned account, the user must fund the account or pay the rent through the instruction. In practice, before sending a create account instruction, check the user's wallet balance and warn them if they lack sufficient SOL. For example, creating a counter account requires paying enough lamports so that the new account is rent-exempt; if the wallet lacks those lamports the transaction will fail. A common mistake is assuming a user has funds; always surface the fee estimate and require confirmation. Anchor does not automatically top up wallets — it relies on the transaction inputs you construct. Implement a small balance check using connection. getBalance and present a clear error message or a link to funding instructions. The takeaway: proactively check balances and explain fees so users know why a wallet approval may request SOL. This reduces failed attempts and improves trust in your DApp. Handling transaction fees and rent means check wallet balance before creating accounts; transactions fail without enough sol for compute and rent-exempt balances.. In practical terms, ensure users have sol for compute and account creation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: AnchorProvider and wallet integration
screens.narratorSegment: AnchorProvider is the glue that lets anchor. Program use your Connection and the connected wallet to sign and send transactions. It accepts a Connection instance, a wallet-like object that exposes publicKey and sendTransaction, and options like commitment. In React, you commonly get these from useConnection and useWallet. A simple pattern is creating provider = new anchor. AnchorProvider(connection, { publicKey, sendTransaction } as any, { commitment: 'confirmed' }); then passing it to new anchor. Program. The provider's role is to hand the built transaction to the wallet for signing and to submit the signed transaction using the underlying Connection. A common trap is type mismatches in TypeScript; many examples use a cast to any as a pragmatic workaround. Another misconception is that the provider itself performs signing; it delegates signing to the wallet. Always treat the wallet as the authority on signatures and do not store private keys in the client. As a takeaway, keep your provider creation centralized in a hook or provider component so all program calls share the same signing and connection behavior, and consider adding retry logic for network hiccups or temporary timeouts.

keyIdea.title: Component pattern
keyIdea.text: Create a provider, instantiate program, derive PDAs, call program.methods for create and increment, and show clear UI feedback for each step.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Build Counter component
Starter structure
// key parts shown in the chapter
import { useConnection, useWallet } from '@solana/wallet-adapter-react';
import * as anchor from '@coral-xyz/anchor';
import idl from '../idl/counter.json';

const provider = new anchor.AnchorProvider(connection, { publicKey, sendTransaction } as any, { commitment: 'confirmed' });
const program = new anchor.Program(idl as anchor.Idl, programId, provider);

// derive PDA
const [counterPda] = PublicKey.findProgramAddressSync(
  [Buffer.from('counter'), publicKey.toBuffer()],
  program.programId
);

// create
await program.methods.create().accounts({ counterAccount: counterPda, user: publicKey, systemProgram: anchor.web3.SystemProgram.programId }).rpc();

// increment
await program.methods.increment().accounts({ counterAccount: counterPda, user: publicKey }).rpc();
Example flow

User connects wallet, clicks create, approves the wallet popup, then approves subsequent increment transactions.

Common error

Calling increment before creating the counter account will fail. Validate presence of counterAccount and surface clear instructions to the user.

Try this

Add a Decrement instruction to the program and a button in the component that follows the same provider → program → methods pattern.

screens.title: Common mistakes and how to diagnose them
screens.narratorSegment: Knowing how to diagnose failures is as important as writing happy-path code. Here are common errors you will see and how to reason about them. Missing signer: happens when the instruction requires an account with isSigner: true and the client did not provide it or the provided account did not sign. For example, forgetting to include the user's publicKey as an account will cause this error. Incorrect program ID: using the wrong programId means the cluster can't find your program; the transaction may be rejected or behave unexpectedly. IDL mismatch: if your local IDL does not match the deployed program, Anchor will serialize data incorrectly and the program may reject it. Insufficient funds: transactions that create accounts or require compute can fail if the wallet lacks SOL for fees or rent. Timeouts and congestion: network delays can cause transactions to take longer or even be dropped; implement retry logic and provide user feedback. For each failure, log the full error, show a human-readable message, and suggest a concrete remediation: recheck accounts, update IDL, top up balance, or retry. The takeaway: pair clear UI feedback with server-side logs or devtools so you can diagnose failures quickly and help users resolve them.

Common errors

Pair precise error logging with clear user messaging so you can diagnose and fix common transaction failures efficiently.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how a connected React DApp calls a deployed Solana program. We'll follow a simple, practical path: install Anchor's client library, import the program IDL, create an AnchorProvider that uses the user's wallet to sign, and call instructions like create and increment on a counter program. This matter: calling programs is the moment your front end triggers immutable on-chain logic, so correctness and clear feedback matter. For example, when your user clicks to create a counter account, the app derives a program-owned address, builds the instruction, and asks the wallet to sign and submit it. A common misconception is that Anchor magically hides all account requirements; Anchor helps but you still must supply correct accounts, enough SOL for fees and rent, and the proper program ID. By the end of this chapter you will be able to wire a React component to an Anchor program, interpret common errors such as missing signers or IDL mismatches, and design retry and feedback flows for users. Think about how you will surface errors to a user who signs a transaction that later times out.

By the end of this chapter you will construct and sign Solana transactions from a React client, use Anchor's client library to call program instructions, and manage confirmation, errors, and fees. Start with the practical: learning how Anchor converts your IDL into methods that build instructions, and how AnchorProvider wraps a Connection and your wallet's send function to sign and submit those transactions. For example, when you call program. methods. create(). accounts({...}). rpc(), Anchor uses the IDL to serialize arguments, but the connected wallet must still approve signing. A common misconception is assuming Anchor removes the need to supply accounts; Anchor needs the correct accounts listed in the IDL and correct program IDs. You'll also practice deriving PDAs for program-owned state and checking balances to cover rent and fees. Finally, you'll learn how to handle typical failure modes such as missing signer errors or IDL mismatches and surface clear messages to users. These skills let you move from reading on-chain data to actively updating program state in a secure, user-friendly way.

This page translates objectives into concrete DApp tasks you will practice. First, construct a Transaction and attach one or more instructions. For example, derive a counter program PDA and add the create instruction before asking the wallet to sign. Second, configure Anchor by installing @coral-xyz/anchor and importing the program IDL JSON; you will instantiate new anchor. Program with the IDL, the program's PublicKey, and an AnchorProvider. Third, send instructions with program. methods... rpc() and wait for confirmation. In practice this means you will implement clear user messages: when creating an account show 'approve transaction' and when incrementing show 'waiting for confirmation'. Fourth, detect and explain errors: missing signer errors usually mean an account declared as isSigner: true was not passed. A common trap is using an outdated IDL after program changes. These objective-to-task mappings will guide your lab work so you can both write code and explain failures to users.

This screen walks through the exact setup you need to call Anchor programs from React. Start by installing the client library with npm install @coral-xyz/anchor; this gives you anchor. Program and AnchorProvider utilities. The IDL is a JSON description of your program's instructions, accounts, and types. You typically copy the compiled file from target/idl into src/idl so your front-end can import it. To create a program client, you need three items: the IDL, the program's PublicKey, and an AnchorProvider. The AnchorProvider wraps your Connection and the wallet's sendTransaction so Anchor can request signing and submission. A concrete example: create a provider from the useConnection and useWallet hooks, then call new anchor. Program(idl, programId, provider). A common misconception is that passing a null provider is fine for read operations; while read-only RPC calls can use Connection directly, anchor. Program requires the provider to sign transactions invoked by methods. As a takeaway, treat the IDL as your contract's surface and AnchorProvider as the bridge that connects that surface to the user's wallet and the cluster. How will you organize your imports so the IDL and provider are available where you need them?

Let's trace the complete lifecycle of a user-triggered action. First, the DApp responds to a user action — for example, clicking 'Create Counter Account.' The app derives any PDAs and gathers the required PublicKeys from the IDL. Second, the app uses anchor. Program or raw web3 constructs to build one or more instructions and adds them to a Transaction object. Third, the app requests the connected wallet to sign the transaction. The wallet may display a confirmation pop-up showing fees and required signatures. Fourth, the wallet returns a signed transaction and your app sends it to the Solana cluster via Connection. Finally, the app waits for confirmation with a commitment level such as 'confirmed' and reports success or error. A concrete example: creating a counter account derives counterPda from seed ["counter", userPubkey], then calls program. methods. create(). accounts({ counterAccount: counterPda, user: userPubkey }). rpc(); Anchor handles serialization, but the wallet must sign. A common misconception is that transaction submission is instantaneous; network congestion or missing funds can delay or fail the transaction. As a takeaway, design your UI to show approval, pending confirmation, and clear failure messages so the user understands each stage.

Program Derived Addresses, or PDAs, are deterministic public keys generated from a program ID and a set of seeds. They are commonly used to create program-owned accounts without a private key. In our counter example, the PDA is derived from the seed bytes of the string 'counter' plus the user's public key. Concretely, the code calls PublicKey. findProgramAddressSync([Buffer. from('counter'), publicKey. toBuffer()], program. programId) and receives the PDA and bump. PDAs matter because they let the program control the account while letting the client deterministically find the address. A common misconception is to treat a PDA like a user-owned key; a PDA cannot sign like a regular keypair — instead the program acts on it. If you provide the wrong seeds or program ID when deriving the PDA, the client and program will refer to different addresses and transactions will fail. As a takeaway, always derive PDAs the same way in both client and program, document your seeds, and verify the PDA on-chain after creation so your front end can safely reference it. Program Derived Addresses (PDAs) means pdas are deterministic, program-owned addresses derived from seeds and the program id; they let programs own state without a private key.. In practical terms, deterministic, program-owned accounts used for state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Anchor exposes an intuitive method chain for calling instructions: program. methods. (...). accounts(...). rpc(). This chain does several things: it serializes arguments according to the IDL, it sets the accounts required by the instruction, and it uses the AnchorProvider to sign and submit the transaction. For example, calling program. methods. create(). accounts({ counterAccount: counterPda, user: publicKey, systemProgram: anchor. web3. SystemProgram. programId, }). rpc() will build the instruction to create the counter account, request the user's signature, and await confirmation. A common mistake is omitting an account declared as isSigner: true in the IDL; this raises a missing signer error because the program expected that signature. Another gotcha is an IDL mismatch — if the on-chain program changed but your local IDL did not, the serialization will be wrong. When using rpc(), provide clear UI messaging: show an approval prompt, then a pending state, and finally success or a human-readable error. As a takeaway, rely on program. methods for convenience, but always double-check required accounts and keep your IDL in sync with deployed programs. Calling program.methods(...).rpc() means program.methods.<name>().accounts(...).rpc() serializes data from the idl, requests wallet signing via the provider, and submits the transaction.. In practical terms, how anchor turns idl methods into signed rpcs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Anchor simplifies client-side interaction by generating type-safe method calls from your IDL, which reduces the need to manually serialize instruction data. Using anchor. Program gives you program. methods. (). accounts(...). rpc() that handles serialization, instruction creation, and uses the provided AnchorProvider to sign and send. In contrast, manual calls with @solana/web3. js require you to build TransactionInstruction objects, manually pack argument bytes, and manage which accounts are writable or signers. A concrete example: incrementing a counter using Anchor is a few chained calls and an rpc() call. Doing the same with web3. js means constructing the instruction data buffer exactly as the program expects. A common misconception is that Anchor removes the need to understand accounts and serialization; it does not. Anchor reduces boilerplate but you still must supply correct accounts and understand program constraints. Use Anchor for faster development and clearer client code; use manual web3. js when you need full control over bytes, custom serialization, or when interacting with programs that do not provide an IDL. The takeaway: prefer Anchor for Anchor-based programs, but keep familiarity with raw web3. js for edge cases and debugging.

Transactions on Solana require small SOL payments to cover compute and the rent-exempt balance for new accounts. When your DApp creates a program-owned account, the user must fund the account or pay the rent through the instruction. In practice, before sending a create account instruction, check the user's wallet balance and warn them if they lack sufficient SOL. For example, creating a counter account requires paying enough lamports so that the new account is rent-exempt; if the wallet lacks those lamports the transaction will fail. A common mistake is assuming a user has funds; always surface the fee estimate and require confirmation. Anchor does not automatically top up wallets — it relies on the transaction inputs you construct. Implement a small balance check using connection. getBalance and present a clear error message or a link to funding instructions. Knowing how to diagnose failures is as important as writing happy-path code. Here are common errors you will see and how to reason about them. Missing signer: happens when the instruction requires an account with isSigner: true and the client did not provide it or the provided account did not sign. For example, forgetting to include the user's publicKey as an account will cause this error. Incorrect program ID: using the wrong programId means the cluster can't find your program; the transaction may be rejected or behave unexpectedly. IDL mismatch: if your local IDL does not match the deployed program, Anchor will serialize data incorrectly and the program may reject it. Insufficient funds: transactions that create accounts or require compute can fail if the wallet lacks SOL for fees or rent. Timeouts and congestion: network delays can cause transactions to take longer or even be dropped; implement retry logic and provide user feedback. For each failure, log the full error, show a human-readable message, and suggest a concrete remediation: recheck accounts, update IDL, top up balance, or retry. The takeaway: pair clear UI feedback with server-side logs or devtools so you can diagnose failures quickly and help users resolve them.
